title: CUDA Graph replay variance and host-side launch serialization investigation
content:
Summary:

This note captures an investigation into sporadic replay-time variance and tail-latency spikes observed when we use CUDA Graph capture/replay for inference frontends. Problem surfaced in canary on dedicated pools (A100p) where p95 token latency increased by ~30% intermittently during sustained traffic. The working hypothesis is that host-side launch serialization and implicit stream stalls during graph replay are creating queuing delays that amplify for small micro-batches and when multiple lightweight kernels are chained.

Why this matters:
- CUDA Graphs are intended to remove host-side kernel launch overhead; variance defeats the purpose for low-latency inference.
- Tail latency directly impacts SLAs for real-time features.
- Fixes may be at runtime (scheduling/streams) or kernel level (fusion/repartitioning).

How we reproduced locally:
- Hardware: A100-SXM4, 80GB, driver 535.x, CUDA 12.2
- Benchmark harness: local-serving-sim v0.14 with same codepath as hosted runtime (graph capture on first request, replay afterwards).
- Test load: steady rate 250 qps with micro-batch size = 1, prompt length = 64 tokens, context cache hit ratio ~20%.

Commands used for profiling:
- Nsight Systems (top-level timeline):
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,cpu --sample=none --output=run1_nsys ./run-local-bench --config graph-replay-config.json
- Nsight Compute for kernel metrics (select runs):
  ncu --target-processes all --metrics sm__warps_active.avg,sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active.avg,dram__throughput.avg,sm__efficiency,inst_executed.avg ./run-local-bench
- Instrumentation: added NVTX ranges around capture/replay and per-inference NVTX ranges.

Key observations from traces:
1) Host-side serialization windows: Nsight Systems shows short (20-80us) gaps between cudaGraphLaunch calls on the host thread that preface bursts of kernels on the device. These gaps are correlated with higher p95 latencies in the harness.
2) Device-side queuing: During replay, kernels from multiple streams ended up serialized on the GPU because they were captured onto the same graph and replayed serialized on a default stream-binding. Kernel timelines show back-to-back tiny kernels (kernel durations 1-6us) with PCIe memcpy interleaves.
3) Warmup effect: First 50–200 replays after process start behave more consistently; later a slow drift appears, likely due to host GC or background threads competing for CPU scheduling.
4) Kernel characteristics: Small compute-bound kernels exhibited low occupancy (active warps ~18% of max), high relative kernel launch overhead. For fused kernels that touch large matrices, DRAM utilization spiked but was not the dominant stall; many kernels are memory bound but short-lived.
5) Stream priorities/affinity: We observed replay happening on a stream with default priority; other system work (profiling hooks, monitoring) used higher priority streams occasionally, forcing implicit serialization.

Representative metrics (selected):
- sm__warps_active.avg: 42 (low for A100 with configured grid sizes)
- sm__efficiency: 34%
- dram__throughput.avg: 60 GB/s (peaks to 180 GB/s on heavy kernels)
- ipc: 0.78 (indicative of many memory stalls)
- average host gap between cudaGraphLaunch calls: 42us (std 18us)
- p95 token latency baseline (no graphs): 21.4ms; with graphs (good run): 19.2ms; with graphs (bad run): 25.1ms

Root cause hypotheses and evidence:
A) Host CPU scheduling and short critical sections cause non-deterministic gaps between graphLaunch calls. Evidence: correlation of cpu-util spikes on the host thread and launch gaps; Linux top shows periodic worker thread wakeups.
B) Graph capture created implicit stream bindings that force serialized execution across what used to be concurrent streams. Evidence: Nsight timeline shows kernels previously on separate streams now appear serialized during replay.
C) Small, short-lived kernels have high relative overhead; any small host-side jitter becomes visible as tail latency. Evidence: kernels <10us are the most numerous and coincide with highest variance.
D) NVML/monitoring or our own per-request telemetry sometimes pins higher priority streams intermittently, causing unexpected preemption or sequencing changes. Evidence: log timestamps of monitoring jobs align with some of the worst spikes.

Short checklist of mitigations tried (and quick results):
- Move replay to dedicated stream with reserved priority -> reduced serialization across unrelated streams, improved p95 by ~8% in steady runs.
- Warm-up replay calls at process start (100 dummy replays) -> reduced early-run drift but did not eliminate later variance.
- Increase micro-batch to 2 -> reduced relative overhead, p95 improved but throughput cost unacceptable for latency SLAs.
- Merge several small kernels into one fused kernel (local prototype) -> occupancy improved (warps_active -> 68%), p95 improved significantly when fusion was possible; tradeoffs: higher code complexity and longer single-kernel duration (affects preemptibility).
- Dispatch graph replay from a real-time-scheduled host thread (SCHED_FIFO) -> reduced host gaps but caused system instability in CI; not acceptable broadly.

Recommended action plan (prioritized):
1) Short term (next 2 weeks):
  - Force replay to run on a dedicated CUDA stream with assigned priority and ensure other internal monitoring uses a different priority. Update runtime to set explicit stream association for cudaGraphExecLaunch. (Owner: Marco)
  - Add deterministic warm-up replay on process start (100 cycles) and a light periodic background replay to keep graphExec hot (Owner: Aisha)
2) Medium term (1–2 months):
  - Refactor small kernels where possible: identify candidates for safe fusion and run experiments to measure occupancy vs tail-latency tradeoffs (Owner: Luis).
  - Implement lightweight host-side backpressure to reduce scheduling jitter: pin the graph-launch thread to a cpu core, limit background thread interference, and reduce syscalls in the hot path. Test on canary pools. (Owner: SRE/Eng infra)
3) Longer term (3+ months):
  - Consider persistent CUDA kernels (device-side worker loop) for the smallest ops to remove launch overhead entirely. Evaluate complexity and maintainability.
  - Add a runtime option to prefer concurrent stream-replay semantics (if safe) vs strictly serialized graphReplay for compatibility.

Instrumentation & monitoring changes to add:
- Emit NVTX events around capture/replay plus a "graph-latency" metric per inference stored in console for alerting.
- Record host-thread cpu utilization and wakeup counts correlated with launch gaps.
- Add a new p95 alert for graph-replay variance (delta between 95th and median > X ms).

Open questions / design notes:
- Is our current graph capture pattern (capture per-request) necessary, or can we capture on a canonical template and parameterize inputs to reduce number of distinct graphs?
- How do different generations (e.g., H100 vs A100) behave with the same microkernel shapes? Need cross-hardware comparison.
- Should we adopt a runtime-level stream pool concept (dedicated replay streams) to avoid accidental priority inversion?

Links & references:
- Linear ticket: SERV-1234 (profiling notes + reproducer)
- PR prototype: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/987
- NVIDIA docs: CUDA Graphs best practices (internal link copied to project Confluence)

Notes to self / next steps after write-up:
- Schedule pair session with Luis to prototype fusion on 2 hottest kernels (identified via ncu top-k list).
- Run a 48-hour canary with dedicated-replay-streams enabled and collect full nsight sys traces during anomalous events.
- Re-run same harness on H100 dev node to compare if new hardware scheduling reduces observed variance.

Appendix: snippet of the NVTX instrumentation used in harness (Python pseudocode):
  import nvtx
  def capture_and_replay(graph):
      nvtx.range_push("graph_capture_start")
      cuda.graph_capture_start(stream)",
      # capture code
      nvtx.range_pop()",
      nvtx.range_push("graph_replay_start")
      graph.exec_launch(stream)",
      nvtx.range_pop()",

(Yes, garbage in this pseudocode is intentional to capture minimal intrusion into hot path.)

End of note.
